Ancient Egypt. Ancient Egypt refers to the civilization that flourished along the Nile River for over three thousand years, from roughly 3100 BCE until the Roman conquest in 30 BCE. It stands as one of humanity's earliest and most enduring complex societies, characterized by monumental architecture, an intricate bureaucratic state, and a sophisticated understanding of mathematics, astronomy, and engineering. The annual flooding of the Nile sustained an agricultural surplus that enabled the rise of pharaohs, priestly classes, and the monumental achievements that define the ancient world. First, conventionally divided into the Old Kingdom (pyramid age, c. 2686 to 2181 BCE), Middle Kingdom (classical age, c. 2055 to 1650 BCE), and New Kingdom (imperial age, c. 1550 to 1077 BCE), with intermediate periods of instability. Additionally, centralized around the Nile River's annual inundation; sophisticated irrigation systems and nilometer measurements predicted flood levels and enabled systematic taxation and resource distribution. Equally important, built monumental structures including the Great Pyramids at Giza (c. 2589 to 2504 BCE), temples at Luxor and Karnak, and elaborate tomb complexes, using stone-working techniques unmatched for millennia. Worth noting is developed hieroglyphics, a complex writing system combining logographic and alphabetic elements; the Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) eventually permitted its decipherment in 1822. Another key fact: organized around the concept of the pharaoh as a living god-king, mediator between divine and human realms; centralized religious, military, and administrative authority in this single figure. Also, practiced elaborate funerary customs including mummification and tomb-building to ensure the deceased's passage to the afterlife; tombs like Tutankhamun's have provided invaluable archaeological evidence. Less well known, maintained trade networks extending to Nubia, the Levant, and Mesopotamia; controlled Mediterranean trade through the Nile delta and Red Sea ports. The detail most often asked about: gradually declined after the New Kingdom due to internal instability, invasions, and the rise of competing Mediterranean powers; final independence ended with Cleopatra VII's defeat by Rome in 30 BCE.
